cards.heading: Split only when the pain is real
cards.hook: Only split a service when the pain of the monolith exceeds the complexity cost of distribution.
cards.body: Splitting too early, or along the wrong boundaries, creates more problems than it solves.

cards.heading: Natural split points have minimal cross-calls
cards.hook: The best place to split a service is wherever two modules already have the fewest calls between them.
cards.body: High cohesion inside a module plus low coupling to the rest of the service is what makes a boundary viable.

cards.heading: A shard key choice is basically permanent
cards.hook: Changing a shard key later means a full data migration, so choose it based on actual query patterns, not convenience.

cards.heading: Consistent hashing is what makes rebalancing cheap
cards.hook: Consistent hashing means adding a new shard only moves the keys that actually belong on it, not the entire dataset.

cards.heading: Cross-shard queries are the expensive part
cards.hook: A query spanning multiple shards needs fan-out and aggregation — design your schema to minimize how often that happens.
cards.body: Co-locating related data, like a user and their orders, on the same shard avoids most of this.

cards.heading: Read replicas target where the load actually is
cards.hook: Most applications run a 90:10 or 95:5 read-to-write ratio, which is exactly why separating reads onto replicas is such high-leverage work.

cards.heading: Replica lag means your own write can look missing
cards.hook: A read replica can trail the primary by seconds, so a user can briefly see stale data right after they wrote something.
cards.body: Reading from the primary immediately after a write is the usual fix when that staleness isn't acceptable.

cards.heading: Events decouple services at the cost of instant consistency
cards.hook: Publishing an event instead of calling a service directly means publishers never need to know who's listening — but operations now complete asynchronously.
cards.body: That's why event handlers must be idempotent: the same message can and will be delivered more than once.

cards.heading: A dead letter queue is the failure valve
cards.hook: Retry a failed message with exponential backoff, and only after it still fails repeatedly does it land in a dead letter queue for a human to look at.

cards.heading: Conway's Law is not optional
cards.hook: Your system architecture ends up mirroring your team's communication structure whether you plan it that way or not.

cards.heading: Clear ownership prevents a 3am dead end
cards.hook: Without a registry mapping each service to a team, an SLA, and an on-call rotation, incidents become everyone's problem and no one's responsibility.

cards.heading: Progressive rollout limits blast radius
cards.hook: Rolling a new version out at 1%, then 10%, then 50%, then 100% means a bug only ever affects a small slice of users before it's caught.

cards.heading: Health checks must watch business metrics
cards.hook: A health check that only confirms the service is responding will miss a conversion-rate drop or a payment failure spike — check the metrics that actually matter.

cards.heading: Feature flags decouple deploy from release
cards.hook: Shipping code behind a flag means you can deploy anytime and decide who sees it later — testing in production with real data before anyone else sees it.

cards.heading: Consistent hashing keeps a rollout stable
cards.hook: A 10% rollout should mean the same 10% of users every time, not a different random slice on every request — consistent hashing by user id is what guarantees that.

cards.heading: Flag sprawl is a real cost
cards.hook: Old flags that outlive their rollout quietly accumulate and slow the system down — remove a flag the moment its rollout completes.

cards.heading: Layered caching can cut database load 99%
cards.hook: Stacking a memory cache, Redis, and a CDN in front of a database took one product catalog from 10,000 database queries a second down to 100.

cards.heading: Invalidation is the hardest part of caching
cards.hook: Multi-layer caching only works if every layer gets invalidated together — miss one key on a write and users start seeing stale data.

cards.heading: Batching turns an N+1 bug into one query
cards.hook: Fetching a user per order in a loop means 101 queries for 100 orders — a DataLoader batches that into 2 queries and turns 505ms into 10ms.

cards.heading: One composite index can fix a 2.5 second query
cards.hook: A query filtering on customer_id and status went from a 2,500ms full table scan to a 15ms index scan with one composite index covering both columns.

cards.heading: An SLO defines how much failure is acceptable
cards.hook: A 99.9% uptime target over 30 days means exactly 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime — that's your error budget to spend.

cards.heading: An exhausted error budget freezes deployments
cards.hook: When the error budget hits zero, deployments stop automatically until reliability recovers — an objective trigger instead of a political argument.

cards.heading: Autoscaling beats static provisioning hard
cards.hook: Running 20 instances around the clock to cover peak load cost $146K a month — autoscaling down during off-peak hours cut that to $58K.

cards.heading: Low utilization is where the waste hides
cards.hook: A service sitting under 30% CPU or memory utilization for weeks is money being spent on capacity nobody's using.

cards.heading: Cost per transaction reveals inefficient code
cards.hook: Total infrastructure cost hides which service is actually wasteful — cost per request or per transaction exposes it.

cards.heading: An ADR records why, not just what
cards.hook: An Architecture Decision Record captures the context, the decision, and the consequences so a future engineer never has to re-litigate a settled choice.

cards.heading: Debt reduction needs a fixed allocation
cards.hook: Allocating a fixed slice of every sprint, like 20%, to tech debt is the only thing that reliably gets it addressed.
cards.body: Without a dedicated allocation, debt reduction always loses to the next feature deadline.

cards.heading: Blameless postmortems fix the system, not the person
cards.hook: A postmortem that assigns blame teaches people to hide mistakes — one that focuses on action items teaches the system to get safer.

cards.heading: Scaling is a checklist, not one fix
cards.hook: Sharding, multi-layer caching, circuit breakers, SLOs, and a tested rollback path all have to exist together — missing any one of them becomes the next incident.

cards.heading: Reserved and spot instances layer on top of autoscaling
cards.hook: Reserved instances cover your predictable baseline at a discount, spot instances handle interruptible batch work cheaply, and autoscaling handles everything variable in between.

cards.heading: Engineers underestimate by default
cards.hook: Optimism bias makes engineers underestimate by 30-50% on average, especially for anything unfamiliar.

cards.heading: Story points measure complexity, not hours
cards.hook: A 5-point story being five times harder than a 1-point one has nothing to do with calendar time — that's exactly why it doesn't read as a deadline.

cards.heading: Fibonacci spacing kills false precision
cards.hook: The gaps between 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 widen on purpose, so you literally can't claim something is an 11 — you're forced to decide 8 or 13.

cards.heading: Three-point estimation turns a guess into a number
cards.hook: (optimistic plus four times realistic plus pessimistic) divided by six gives you a defensible expected time instead of a single confident-sounding guess.

cards.heading: Unestimable work is just undecomposed work
cards.hook: Any task that feels impossible to estimate just hasn't been broken down to 1-3 day pieces yet.

cards.heading: A breakdown's real value is visibility
cards.hook: A work breakdown structure's biggest win isn't the total number, it's that stakeholders can see exactly what's included and choose what to cut.

cards.heading: Give a size plus a plan to narrow it
cards.hook: When requirements aren't clear yet, a t-shirt size like Large-to-Extra-Large plus a one-week feasibility study beats inventing a fake precise number.

cards.heading: The cone of uncertainty narrows as you learn
cards.hook: At week zero your estimate can be off by 4x — by the time the design is done, that range has tightened to maybe 1.5x.

cards.heading: Risk multipliers stack multiplicatively
cards.hook: New technology, legacy code, and unclear requirements each add their own percentage buffer, and those buffers compound — 30 days can become 85 days once you multiply them all together.

cards.heading: Never give a single number
cards.hook: "25-35 days, most likely 30" is more honest than "30 days" and gives stakeholders a real sense of the uncertainty involved.

cards.heading: An estimate is not a commitment
cards.hook: An estimate is your best professional judgment; a commitment is a promise with a deliberate buffer built on top of it.

cards.heading: Confidence level matters as much as the number
cards.hook: Stating whether you're high, medium, or low confidence tells a stakeholder exactly how much weight to put on your estimate.

cards.heading: The hero assumption inflates every estimate
cards.hook: Estimating from your best-ever day, with zero meetings or interruptions, is exactly why real work always takes longer than planned.

cards.heading: Coding time is a fraction of the real project
cards.hook: Requirements, design, testing, review, and documentation routinely add up to more time than the coding itself — a 10-day coding estimate is often a 25-day project.

cards.heading: Track your estimates against reality
cards.hook: Recording your original estimate, the actual time, and what you missed after every project is the only way your calibration actually improves.

cards.heading: Your job shifts from coding to communicating
cards.hook: Junior engineers spend roughly 80% of their time coding; tech leads spend roughly 80% communicating — impact scales through other people, not through more code.

cards.heading: The same fact needs four different framings
cards.hook: A slow API gets explained in N+1 queries and DataLoader to engineers, in timeline and risk to your manager, and in customer impact alone to an executive.

cards.heading: Write for scanning, not reading
cards.hook: A wall of text buries the actual ask — bold headers, bullets, and a specific question at the end get an answer.

cards.heading: Yes, and beats no, but
cards.hook: Building a cheaper version of someone's idea keeps the conversation open — shooting it down with a list of obstacles just shuts it down.

cards.heading: Disagree with data, not opinion
cards.hook: Citing the actual numbers behind your concern, then asking what you're missing, lands better than a flat dismissal of someone's suggestion.

cards.heading: Questions are less confrontational than statements
cards.hook: "What problem does this solve that the simpler option doesn't?" gets further than "that's overcomplicated" — questions often lead people to find the flaw themselves.

cards.heading: An analogy beats jargon for non-technical audiences
cards.hook: Explaining a race condition as "multiple cooks working the same order without coordinating" lands where "vector clocks aren't converging" doesn't.

cards.heading: Not knowing is fine, going silent isn't
cards.hook: "I don't have enough context, I'll check and get back to you by end of day" beats both guessing and freezing up in a meeting.

cards.heading: Report a mistake in minutes, not after discovery
cards.hook: An immediate message with what happened, current status, and the next update time rebuilds trust far faster than hoping no one notices.

cards.heading: A spec and a deadline beat a vague ask
cards.hook: "Can you add an endpoint ASAP" gets deprioritized — a concrete spec, a real deadline with buffer, and an offer to help gets scheduled.

cards.heading: Blockers are the most valuable line in a status update
cards.hook: Surfacing a blocker before it becomes a missed deadline is the entire point of a weekly update — burying it defeats the purpose.

cards.heading: Non-goals matter as much as goals
cards.hook: A design doc's non-goals section tells readers exactly what you're deliberately not solving, heading off a whole category of scope debate later.

cards.heading: Situation, behavior, impact, suggestion
cards.hook: Critical feedback structured as situation, behavior, impact, and suggestion reads as a fixable problem, not a verdict on someone's ability.

cards.heading: The mysterious Slack ping wastes everyone's time
cards.hook: "Got a minute?" and then silence forces a guessing game — stating the actual question upfront gets a faster, better answer.

cards.heading: Unreasonable stakeholders are optimizing differently
cards.hook: A PM pushing a deadline and an SRE blocking a release aren't being difficult — they're each maximizing a success metric that isn't yours.

cards.heading: Different roles optimize for different metrics
cards.hook: A PM measures features shipped, DevOps measures uptime, an executive measures revenue — knowing which one you're talking to changes what argument actually works.

cards.heading: Ask scope questions before you estimate
cards.hook: "Add two-factor authentication" hides a dozen unscoped decisions — which methods, mandatory or optional, account recovery — surface them before committing to a number.

cards.heading: Every scope addition is a trade-off, not a freebie
cards.hook: The moment new scope appears, state it explicitly as more time or less of something else — silently absorbing it is how a 3-week project becomes 7 weeks.

cards.heading: Offer an alternative, don't just refuse
cards.hook: A smaller version in the original timeline, or the full version with more time, both beat a flat "no" to an urgent request.

cards.heading: Triage conflicting urgent requests in five minutes
cards.hook: Ranking three simultaneous fires by actual business impact and communicating the order immediately beats context-switching between all three badly.

cards.heading: Own your own 1-on-1 agenda
cards.hook: Bringing wins, blockers, career goals, and feedback to a 1-on-1 yourself gets far more out of it than waiting for your manager to ask.

cards.heading: Surface risk the week you spot it
cards.hook: Flagging a risk early, with options already attached, gives your manager time to adjust — surfacing it after it's already a missed deadline doesn't.

cards.heading: PMs need the underlying need, not the stated solution
cards.hook: "We need custom reports" usually means five customers manually exporting to Excel — solve that need with three cost-tiered options, not a single huge build.

cards.heading: Question a bad priority with data, not dismissal
cards.hook: Bringing concrete numbers and asking what you're missing opens a dialogue — calling a priority stupid just ends one.

cards.heading: The elevator pitch is bottom line, then impact, then ask
cards.hook: An executive needs the proposal and the business reason in 30 seconds — the technical detail only comes up if they actually ask for it.

cards.heading: An 8-hour day isn't 8 hours of coding
cards.hook: Once meetings, Slack, and context switching are subtracted, a typical day leaves 2-3 hours of actual deep focus time.

cards.heading: An interruption costs more than its own length
cards.hook: Each interruption costs 10-20 minutes total, not just the time it takes — the rest is spent re-entering the flow you were in before it hit.

cards.heading: Morning blocks work because the day hasn't derailed yet
cards.hook: Protecting the first few hours of the day for deep work beats the afternoon, because fewer people have had the chance to interrupt you yet.

cards.heading: Every yes is a no to something else
cards.hook: Declining a request with a concrete alternative protects your time without actually burning the relationship.

cards.heading: Sort by important, not just urgent
cards.hook: The Eisenhower matrix splits work into do-first, schedule, delegate, and eliminate — most inboxes are dominated by urgent-but-unimportant noise in the delegate and eliminate quadrants.

cards.heading: The two-minute rule clears small tasks instantly
cards.hook: Anything under two minutes should just get done immediately — it prevents a pile of tiny tasks from becoming constant mental overhead.

cards.heading: Batching similar work avoids a context-switch tax
cards.hook: Grouping all meetings into one block and all code review into another means you're not paying the mental cost of switching between types of work all day.

cards.heading: Batching Slack checks keeps you responsive anyway
cards.hook: Checking messages four times a day at scheduled times is still responsive enough, but cuts your context switches from 30-plus a day down to four.

cards.heading: Logging interruptions for a week reveals the pattern
cards.hook: Most teams find 60% or more of their interruptions could have been handled async — you only see that pattern if you actually track it for a week.

cards.heading: Match hard work to your actual peak energy
cards.hook: A morning person and a night owl have inverted peak hours — schedule your hardest problem for whichever window is genuinely yours, not a generic 9-to-5 assumption.

cards.heading: Burnout's warning signs show up before quality does
cards.hook: Dreading opening your laptop and constant exhaustion despite sleep are earlier signals than your actual output dropping — catch it there instead.

cards.heading: A hard stop protects the rest of your life
cards.hook: Setting a firm end time and actually closing the laptop is what makes a sustainable pace sustainable — not working fewer hours in theory.

cards.heading: No agenda is a reason to decline
cards.hook: A meeting invite with no clear decision or goal attached is a signal to push for an async doc instead of accepting it.

cards.heading: Default to 30 minutes, not 60
cards.hook: Most meetings don't actually need a full hour — defaulting to 30 minutes forces a tighter agenda and ends up being enough almost every time.

cards.heading: The five-minute start breaks the freeze
cards.hook: Committing to just five minutes — open the file, write one function signature — is usually enough to build momentum, because starting is the actual hard part.

cards.heading: Rubber duck debugging works for a real reason
cards.hook: Explaining a stuck problem out loud to anyone, or anything, forces you to articulate it clearly enough that the solution often falls out on its own.

cards.heading: Propose an answer, don't just ask a question
cards.hook: An async message with your own proposed answer and a response deadline lets you keep moving if no one objects, instead of waiting on an open-ended question.

cards.heading: A shared doc beats a meeting for most decisions
cards.hook: Writing a doc, collecting async comments, and meeting only if real disagreement remains takes a fraction of the time of defaulting straight to a meeting.
